pages.text: For Basic 9 Career Technology Business Pitch Day, Kwaku, Eyram, and Zuwera formed “Subin Bamboo Craft”, sanding cured local bamboo stems and offcut leather into sleek pen holders and study bookstands. Following the NaCCA entrepreneurial syllabus, they drafted a clear four-part Business Plan: Executive Summary, Product & Workshop Operations, Marketing Plan, and Financial Projections. For a supervised classroom financing comparison, the group estimated GH¢ 2,000.00 in equipment capital over nine months; no student would sign a loan agreement.

pages.text: Next, Kwaku prepared their five-slide Multimedia Presentation for the judges. Remembering Computing presentation design principles, he replaced cramped walls of tiny yellow text on a bright background with high-contrast dark navy headings on soft cream slides, concise five-point bullet summaries, consistent font sizes, and genuine photos of their bamboo curing process, avoiding dizzying sound effects on every line so the judges focused on the engineering and numbers.

Remembering Computing presentation design principles, he replaced cramped walls of tiny yellow text on a bright background with high-contrast dark navy headings on soft cream slides, concise five-point bullet summaries, consistent font sizes, and genuine photos of their bamboo curing process, avoiding dizzying sound effects on every line so the judges focused on the engineering and numbers.

pages.text: Then came the critical financial test. An informal roadside lender had flyers offering “Easy 4% Monthly Flat Interest!”, whereas Mr Mensah’s Teachers & Community Credit Union offered an illustrative, adult-supervised enterprise loan quote at “18% per annum Simple Interest”. Kwaku nearly picked 4% because 4 looked smaller than 18! Zuwera stopped him immediately at the board: “Compare like with like, Kwaku! Four percent of the original principal each month totals 4% × 12 = 48% of that principal over twelve months under this flat-rate assumption! Let us calculate both over 9 months (T = 9/12 = 0.75 years) using the Simple Interest formula: I = (P × R × T) ÷ 100.”
sentences: Then came the critical financial test.

An informal roadside lender had flyers offering “Easy 4% Monthly Flat Interest!”, whereas Mr Mensah’s Teachers & Community Credit Union offered an illustrative, adult-supervised enterprise loan quote at “18% per annum Simple Interest”.
Kwaku nearly picked 4% because 4 looked smaller than 18!
Zuwera stopped him immediately at the board: “Compare like with like, Kwaku!
Four percent of the original principal each month totals 4% × 12 = 48% of that principal over twelve months under this flat-rate assumption!
Let us calculate both over 9 months (T = 9/12 = 0.75 years) using the Simple Interest formula: I = (P × R × T) ÷ 100.”
pages.alt: Zuwera writing a bold warning comparison on whiteboard: 4% per month = 48% per year vs Credit Union 18% per annum, setting up I = (P x R x T) / 100.

pages.text: Zuwera worked both options step by step on Principal P = GH¢ 2,000 for Time T = 9/12 years. Under the Credit Union’s 18% per annum rate: I = (2,000 × 18 × 9) ÷ (100 × 12) = 324,000 ÷ 1,200 = GH¢ 270.00 interest, giving Total Amount A = P + I = GH¢ 2,270.00! Under the informal lender’s 4% monthly flat rate for 9 months: I = 2,000 × (4 ÷ 100) × 9 = GH¢ 720.00 interest, giving a Total Amount of GH¢ 2,720.00, which cost GH¢ 450.00 more! She also checked the registered tool-shop invoice for a GH¢ 1,600 bench drill plus an assumed 15% VAT for this classroom example: 0.15 × 1,600 = GH¢ 240, giving GH¢ 1,840 and leaving GH¢ 160 for sanding belts. Zuwera warned that real Ghanaian invoices must use the applicable tax rules and levies on the transaction date.

pages.text: At Friday’s Pitch Day, Mr Mensah and the panel applauded the team’s accessible HTML catalogue, crisp slides, carefully checked illustrative supplier invoice, and razor-sharp Simple Interest comparison, and offered to review the club’s proposal for a supervised school micro-grant after the required approvals! Watching juniors test their bamboo bookstands in the library, the trio proved that clean code, clear communication, and mathematical vigilance protect young entrepreneurs from debt traps before business even begins.
